entry: English king (r. 1199–1216). The youngest son of [[Henry II of England|Henry II]] and [[Eleanor of Aquitaine]], John was nicknamed Lackland because he was not expected to inherit significant lands. He was proclaimed king after his brother Richard I died in 1199, and [[Philip II of France|Philip II]] recognized his possession of the continental Angevin lands in 1200. Renewed war with France led to the loss of [[Normandy]] and most of his other French lands by 1204, which ended the Angevin Empire. A dispute with [[Pope Innocent III]] over the appointment of the archbishop of Canterbury brought an interdict on England and John's excommunication. A baronial revolt forced him to seal [[Magna Carta]] in 1215, but neither side kept its terms, and civil war followed. John died of [[Dysentery|dysentery]] in eastern England in late 1216. Contemporary chroniclers were largely critical of him, and later historians have debated his record. His reign provided material for Victorian fiction, and he remains a villain in [[Robin Hood]] legends.

Scottish Reformed minister and theologian. Born in Haddington and ordained a Catholic priest, Knox was influenced by George Wishart and was taken prisoner by French forces in 1547. After his release in 1549 he served as a royal chaplain to [[Edward VI]] in the [[Church of England]], where he influenced the text of the Book of Common Prayer. When [[Mary I]] restored Catholicism, he moved to [[Geneva]] and met [[John Calvin]]. He returned to Scotland in 1559 and led the [[Reformation]] there, helping bring about the ousting of Mary of Guise, who had governed Scotland for her daughter. He co-wrote the confession of faith and church order of the new Reformed Church, the Kirk. After [[Mary, Queen of Scots]] was imprisoned, he openly called for her execution. His five-volume *The History of the Reformation in Scotland* was written between 1559 and 1566.

English musician and songwriter. Born in [[Liverpool]], Lennon formed the Quarrymen in 1956, which evolved into [[The Beatles]] in 1960. His songwriting partnership with [[Paul McCartney]] is described as the most successful in history. From 1967, beginning with "All You Need Is Love," his songs became anthems for the counterculture and the anti-war movement. In 1969 he formed the Plastic Ono Band with his second wife, [[Yoko Ono]], and staged a bed-in for peace. His criticism of the [[Vietnam War]] led to a three-year deportation attempt by the Nixon administration. From 1969 to 1975 he had four UK top-10 singles. As a performer, writer or co-writer he had 25 Billboard Hot 100 number-one singles. His album *Double Fantasy* won the 1981 Grammy Award for Album of the Year. He was shot and killed by Mark David Chapman three weeks after the album's release. He was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] twice.

American [[Civil rights movement|civil rights]] leader and U.S. representative. Lewis took part in the 1960 Nashville sit-ins and the Freedom Rides, and chaired the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee from 1963 to 1966. He was one of the "Big Six" leaders who organized the 1963 March on Washington. In 1965 he led the Selma to Montgomery march, which state troopers attacked on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in an incident known as Bloody Sunday. A member of the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]], he represented a district including most of [[Atlanta]] in the [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. House of Representatives]] from 1987 until his death.

Scottish engineer and television pioneer. Born in Helensburgh and educated in [[Glasgow]], Baird was classified unfit for active military service in [[World War I]] and worked on munitions at a power company. In Hastings in the 1920s he built experimental apparatus from improvised parts, and in 1925 he transmitted the first grayscale television picture, of a ventriloquist's dummy. On January 26, 1926, he demonstrated the world's first mechanical television system to members of the Royal Institution in London. His company achieved the first transatlantic television transmission in 1928. In 1929 the [[BBC]] adopted his system for experimental broadcasts. He later developed the first publicly demonstrated color television system and an electronic color picture tube.

[[American football|American football]] coach and broadcaster. Madden coached the Oakland Raiders of the [[National Football League]] from 1969 to 1978, never had a losing season, and won the franchise's first title in [[Super Bowl|Super Bowl XI]]. He had the highest winning percentage among NFL head coaches with at least 100 games. After retiring he was a color commentator for NFL telecasts from 1979 to 2009 and won 16 Sports Emmy Awards. He was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2006. The Madden NFL video game series, for which he lent his name and expertise, became the best-selling American football video game franchise.

British [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative]] prime minister (1990–1997). Major held Cabinet posts under [[Margaret Thatcher]] and succeeded her after the 1990 Conservative leadership election. His government replaced the poll tax with council tax, took part in the [[Gulf War]], and withdrew the pound from the European Exchange Rate Mechanism on Black Wednesday. Two years into his premiership he won a fourth consecutive Conservative election victory, with more than 14 million votes. Divisions over Europe and a shrinking majority weakened his government, and the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]] won the 1997 general election. Major later opposed [[Brexit]] and supported the campaign for the UK to remain in the [[European Union]].

English economist. Originally trained in mathematics at the [[University of Cambridge]], Keynes argued that inadequate aggregate demand could leave economies with prolonged unemployment, because wages are rigid downward. He held that governments should use fiscal and monetary policy to counter recessions and depressions. He set out these ideas in *The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money* (1936), which became the basis of Keynesian economics; leading Western economies had begun adopting his recommendations by the late 1930s. After [[World War II]], as a leader of the British delegation, he helped design postwar international economic institutions, though the American delegation overruled him on several points. His influence waned in the 1970s amid stagflation and criticism from [[Milton Friedman]], but the [[2008 financial crisis]] brought a Keynesian resurgence. His ideas remain foundational to mainstream [[Macroeconomics|macroeconomics]]. He also criticized the reparations of the [[Treaty of Versailles]] in *The Economic Consequences of the Peace* (1919).

British and American computer programmer and businessman. In 1987 he wrote the first commercial anti-virus software and founded McAfee Associates, which he left in 1994 after selling his stake. He later became the company's most vocal critic. His fortunes declined after the [[2008 financial crisis]], and he promoted [[Cryptocurrency|cryptocurrency]] and opposed government [[Surveillance|surveillance]]. He twice sought the Libertarian Party nomination for [[President of the United States|president]], in 2016 and 2020, without success. Facing U.S. tax evasion charges, he was arrested in Spain in 2020. He was found dead in prison there while awaiting extradition, in an apparent [[Suicide|suicide]]; his wife said she did not believe he had died by suicide.

American naval officer and [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] politician. A naval aviator, McCain was shot down over [[Hanoi]] during the [[Vietnam War]] in 1967 and was held as a prisoner of war until 1973, enduring torture. He refused an early release. He represented [[Arizona]] in the [[United States Congress|U.S. Congress]] from 1983, first in the House and from 1987 in the Senate. He lost the 2000 Republican presidential nomination to [[George W. Bush]] and was the party's nominee in 2008, losing to [[Barack Obama]]. He refused to support [[Donald Trump]] in 2016 and later became a critic of his administration.

American former [[Tennis|tennis]] player. McEnroe was ranked world No. 1 in men's singles for 170 weeks and in men's doubles for 269 weeks. His 155 career titles set an Open Era record, and he won seven [[Grand Slam (tennis)|Grand Slam]] singles titles, four at the US Open and three at Wimbledon. Known for his volleying and his confrontational on-court behavior, he contributed to five Davis Cup titles for the United States. He later became a television commentator for major tournaments.

English poet and civil servant. Educated at the [[University of Cambridge|University of Cambridge]], Milton was a pamphleteer during the [[English Civil War]] and later served the Commonwealth of England under its Council of State and then under [[Oliver Cromwell]]. His *Areopagitica* (1644), which condemned pre-publication censorship, is among the most influential defenses of [[Freedom of speech|freedom of speech]]. He went blind from [[Glaucoma|glaucoma]] by 1652 and dictated his later works, including *Paradise Lost* (1667), a twelve-book epic in blank verse on the Fall of Man. Milton introduced many new words into English from [[Latin]] and Ancient Greek. He is widely regarded as one of the greatest English poets, second in influence only to [[William Shakespeare]], though critics including [[T. S. Eliot]] have objected to his work. His republicanism has affected his critical reputation over the centuries.

Scottish-born American naturalist and writer. Born in Dunbar, [[Scotland]], Muir emigrated as a boy to a farm near Portage, [[Wisconsin]]. His books and essays about nature, especially in the [[Sierra Nevada]], were widely read. He co-founded the Sierra Club in 1892 and served as its first president. His articles in *Century Magazine* supported the campaign that led Congress to establish [[Yosemite National Park]] in 1890, and his activism helped preserve Yosemite Valley and Sequoia National Park. A 1903 camping trip in Yosemite with President [[Theodore Roosevelt]] convinced Roosevelt to expand federal protections. Muir opposed the damming of Hetch Hetchy Valley, which was approved in 1913. Known as the "Father of the National Parks," he is an enduring figure in American conservation.

British-American comedian and television host. Oliver began as a [[Stand-up comedy|stand-up]] in the United Kingdom and was the senior British correspondent on *The Daily Show* with [[Jon Stewart]] from 2006 to 2013. Since 2014 he has hosted the [[HBO]] series *Last Week Tonight with John Oliver*, a weekly program of extended investigative segments that has won 20 Emmy Awards and two Peabody Awards. Its influence on policy has been dubbed the "John Oliver effect." He co-hosted the comedy [[Podcast|podcast]] *The Bugle*. He became an American citizen in 2019.

American diplomat and sixth [[President of the United States|president]] of the United States (1825–1829). The eldest son of [[John Adams]], he served as secretary of state under [[James Monroe]] from 1817 to 1825. He negotiated the Adams–Onís Treaty, which acquired Spanish Florida, and helped formulate the [[Monroe Doctrine]]. He led negotiations for the Treaty of Ghent, which ended the [[War of 1812]]. Congress blocked many of his initiatives, and in 1828 he lost the presidential election to [[Andrew Jackson]]. He later served in the U.S. House of Representatives, the only former president to be elected to that chamber, and became a leading opponent of slavery's expansion.

American [[Political philosophy|political philosopher]]. Rawls's theory of "justice as fairness" holds that society should guarantee equal basic liberties and equal opportunity, and should arrange social and economic inequalities to benefit the least advantaged. He argued for these principles with a [[Thought experiment|thought experiment]], the "original position," in which people choose principles without knowing their own place in society. He set out the theory in *A Theory of Justice* (1971), which revived systematic normative political philosophy in English-speaking academia. In *Political Liberalism* (1993) he asked how political power could be legitimately exercised in a society of conflicting moral and religious views. He taught at [[Harvard University]] from 1962 until 1991, and in 1999 President [[Bill Clinton]] presented him with the National Humanities Medal.

American expatriate painter. Considered the leading portrait painter of his generation, Sargent depicted the luxury of the [[Belle Époque]] and Edwardian society. He made roughly 900 oil paintings and more than 2,000 watercolors. Born in [[Florence]] to American parents, he trained in Florence and Paris and lived most of his life in Europe. His *Portrait of Madame X* caused a scandal at the Paris Salon in the 1880s, and he left for England soon afterward. His commissioned portraits followed the grand manner, while his informal studies and landscapes showed the influence of [[Impressionism]]. Later he devoted much energy to [[Mural|mural]] painting and [[Landscape painting|landscape]] work *en plein air*. His travels took him from [[Venice]] to [[Corfu]], Montana and Maine. A 1980s exhibition of his previously hidden male nudes prompted a reevaluation of his work.

English physician and a founder of modern [[Epidemiology|epidemiology]]. Born in [[York]], Snow pioneered anesthesia dosage and inhalation devices for ether and [[Chloroform|chloroform]]. He administered chloroform to [[Queen Victoria]] for her last two childbirths, which helped legitimize its clinical use. During the 1854 [[Cholera]] outbreak in Soho, [[London]], he mapped more than 500 deaths and traced the cluster to the Broad Street pump. The epidemic was already waning when its handle was removed at his urging, and his findings led to changes in London's water and waste systems. His work on [[Hygiene|medical hygiene]] and early germ theory influenced public health far beyond London.

American novelist and journalist. Much of Steinbeck's fiction is set in the Salinas Valley and the California Coast Ranges, and it often portrays migrant workers and the rural poor. His novels include *Tortilla Flat* (1935), *Of Mice and Men* (1937), and *The Grapes of Wrath* (1939), a [[Pulitzer Prize]]–winning portrait of a family's migration during the [[Dust Bowl]] and the [[Great Depression]]. Later works include *Cannery Row* (1945) and *East of Eden* (1952). He worked as a war correspondent in [[World War II]] and the [[Vietnam War]]. He received the 1962 Nobel Prize in Literature and, in 1964, the Presidential Medal of Freedom from [[Lyndon B. Johnson]].

English philosopher and politician. A leading exponent of [[Liberalism|liberalism]], Mill stated the harm principle in *On Liberty* (1859), holding that the state may limit an individual's liberty only to prevent harm to others. He was a proponent of [[Utilitarianism]] in the tradition of [[Jeremy Bentham]], and in *Utilitarianism* (1861) he placed higher value on intellectual pleasures. For many years he worked as an examiner for the [[East India Company]]. As a Member of Parliament for Westminster from 1865 to 1868, he advocated [[Women's suffrage|women's suffrage]] and [[Proportional representation]]. In *The Subjection of Women* (1869) he challenged gender hierarchies with arguments from utility and individual autonomy. *A System of Logic* (1843) formalized empirical methods in [[Scientific method|scientific]] reasoning.

American actor. Travolta rose to fame on the [[Sitcom|sitcom]] *Welcome Back, Kotter* before starring in *Saturday Night Fever* (1977) and *Grease* (1978) with [[Olivia Newton-John]]. He received [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] nominations for Best Actor for *Saturday Night Fever* and for *Pulp Fiction* (1994), directed by [[Quentin Tarantino]]. He converted to [[Scientology]] in 1975. Travolta is also a private pilot.

American filmmaker and writer. Born in [[Baltimore]], Waters rose to fame in the early 1970s with transgressive cult films such as *Pink Flamingos* (1972) and *Female Trouble* (1974). His comedy *Hairspray* (1988) became a Broadway musical and a 2007 film. *Serial Mom* (1994) starred [[Kathleen Turner]]. Waters also works as a visual artist and was twice nominated for a Grammy Award for Best Spoken Word Album. He received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 2023.

American [[Serial killer|serial killer]]. Gacy raped and murdered at least 33 young men and boys between 1972 and 1978 in Norwood Park Township, a suburb of [[Chicago]], Illinois. He lured victims to his home, often by feigning a magic trick with handcuffs, and killed them by [[Asphyxia|asphyxiation]] or strangulation. Known as the "Killer Clown" for his public performances as a clown, he was arrested in December 1978. He was convicted of 33 murders, the most by one individual in United States legal history. Sentenced to death, he was executed by [[Lethal injection|lethal injection]] in Illinois.

American actor. Born Marion Robert Morrison in Winterset, Iowa, Wayne grew up in [[Southern California]] and at first appeared in small parts before playing leads in numerous B movies. His breakthrough came with *Stagecoach* (1939), directed by [[John Ford]]. Known for [[Western (genre)|Westerns]] and war films, he appeared in 179 film and television productions. His other roles include *Red River* (1948), *The Searchers* (1956), *Rio Bravo* (1959) with [[Dean Martin]], and *The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance* (1962) with [[James Stewart]]. He won the [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Actor for *True Grit* (1969) and was posthumously awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1980. A 1971 [[Playboy]] interview drew criticism for his remarks on racial integration.

English cleric and theologian. Wesley led a revival movement within the [[Church of England]] that became [[Methodism]]. At the [[University of Oxford|University of Oxford]] he led the "Holy Club," a group devoted to a devout Christian life. After an unsuccessful ministry in [[Savannah, Georgia|Savannah]], he had an [[Evangelicalism|evangelical]] conversion in 1738 and began to preach outdoors. He traveled widely across Great Britain and Ireland, organizing small groups for accountability and religious instruction, and appointed itinerant, unordained evangelists, both women and men. Under his direction Methodists became leaders in social causes, including the abolition of slavery. Wesley argued against Calvinism and for Christian perfection, and his Wesleyan theology still informs Methodist churches. By the end of his life he was described as the "best-loved man in England."
